target_segments.source_text: Not any pattern he'd ever seen.
"I'll be back soon; we want to be out of the corridor before the light fades, and the clouds are already darkening.
The handwriting was strong and practical through most of the pages—supply lists, wind readings, sketches of these same knots.
They hurried back toward the bridge.

They came down through the mist-filled trees at a dead run and found the great root span hanging from its anchor on the far side, its near anchors torn loose, thrashing in the wind above a drop into the cloud sea.
He got three-quarters of the way across before the near anchor trunk groaned.
The bridge was dropping, and the line was still clipped to his harness, dragging him down with the falling span.
There was only one thing left to do, and he hated every second of it: he unclipped the line from his harness and let it fall away with the bridge, giving up the rope.
The bridge fell away beneath him into the cloud sea, and Arda lunged for the ledge where Nisa waited. She leaned out and hauled; his hand found her wrist, and her grip found him.
"My line," he said, looking at his empty harness.
Arda managed a crooked smile. "Worth it," he said, though it still stung.
He knew only that it had been real, and that the proof was tucked safely with him.
